newsitem.title: CROATIA: Croatia's ailing Tudjman seeks place in history.
newsitem.headline: Croatia's ailing Tudjman seeks place in history.

text.p: Ailing Croatian President Franjo Tudjman is trying to counter criticism of his authoritarian rule before elections and secure a respectable place in history, diplomats said on Thursday.

The 74-year-old leader, said by U.S. sources to have inoperable cancer, delivered an unusually moderate annual "state of the nation" address on Wednesday amid rumours he might announce dramatic changes to the constitution or even his own retirement.
"The speech had a lot of "feel good' news, which is not surprising in an election year," said a Western diplomat.

The authoritarian leader, who steered Croatia to independence from federal Yugoslavia in 1991, ruled out any substantial constitutional changes and made clear the presidential election would take place this year as scheduled.
But he did not say whether he would run for a third term in office and did not mention his illness in the two-hour speech to parliament.

Another diplomat singled out Tudjman's remark that a constitutional amendment should be introduced to enhance Croatia's independence by banning attempts to merge it with any Yugoslav or Balkans state or federation.
"I am inclined to believe it was his effort to reign beyond his grave, to avoid the possibility that some naive future leader might accept a Balkan association," the diplomat said.
"Implicitly, he is concerned if his heritage will be preserved, if Croatia will stay independent," the Western diplomat added.
Tudjman also called for unity of all political parties and failed to lash out against Croatia's foreign and internal enemies, a trademark of his long and often furious speeches of the past.
"He talked about increases in the economy, the need to get to grips with (economic) crime. That clearly aims at election, because that is what has been very unpopular," the diplomat said.
Tudjman's ruling HDZ party, whose popularity hinges on its charismatic leader, faces huge popular discontent over its alleged corruption and mismanagement of economy.
Analysts believe the party would try to avoid presidential elections should Tudjman feel too ill to run, for lack of a popular substitute candidate.

The diplomats praised Tudjman's appeal to minority Serbs in their last rebel enclave of Eastern Slavonia to fully take part in voting for local administrative bodies, after which the enclave is to return to Croatian rule.

Zagreb previously proposed a conciliatory human and minority rights package to the Serbs which the U.N. praised as better than expected but which the Serbs have spurned, demanding the enclave remain a separate administrative unit.

"Tudjman was surprisingly forthcoming to the demands in Eastern Slavonia. That's good and it also serves his purpose -- to secure his place in history as the man who integrated the whole of Croatia," one diplomat said.
